title: The pulseless limb after fracture or dislocation
subtitle: Realign, re-examine, revascularise within the hour

sources.title: BOAST: Diagnosis and management of arterial injuries associated with musculoskeletal trauma

sources.org: National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (NICE)
sources.title: Fractures (complex): assessment and management (NG37)

sources.org: European Society for Vascular Surgery (ESVS), Wahlgren CM et al. Eur J Vasc Endovasc Surg 69:179

sources.org: National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (NICE)
sources.title: Major trauma: assessment and initial management (NG39)

red_flags.text: Hard signs: absent pulse, pulsatile bleeding, expanding or pulsatile haematoma, or a palpable thrill or audible bruit.
A pale, cold limb with slow or absent capillary return distal to the injury.
Loss of sensation and then movement distal to the injury: advanced ischaemia.
Knee dislocation, tibial plateau fracture-dislocation, supracondylar femoral fracture and penetrating injury near a major artery.
There is no safe ischaemic time. The clock started at injury, not at arrival.

do_now.text: Control haemorrhage by direct pressure, wound packing or a tourniquet applied as distally as possible. No blind clamping.
Realign and splint the pulseless deformed limb urgently, then repeat and document the arterial examination.
If the limb remains dysvascular after realignment: consultant input now, and CT angiography concurrently with any whole-body CT.
If hard signs persist after realignment and reduction, explore surgically at once. Do not delay revascularisation for angiography in complex fractures.

assess.text: Compare with the uninjured side. If the injured pulse does not feel the same, suspect an arterial injury until imaging shows otherwise.
Capillary return and a Doppler signal do not exclude an arterial injury.
Ankle-brachial index where the limb allows.
Document peripheral nerve function, the time of injury, and the time perfusion was first found to be abnormal.

investigate.text: CT angiography if the patient is stable enough to scan; on-table angiography if not.
Group and crossmatch, coagulation, lactate and creatine kinase.
Imaging never takes priority over getting a dysvascular limb to theatre.

resuscitate.text: Unstable patients with uncontrolled bleeding undergo resuscitation and surgical intervention simultaneously.
Intravenous tranexamic acid as soon as possible for active or suspected active bleeding in major trauma.

definitive.text: Revascularisation is an emergency procedure (NCEPOD category 1) and should start within one hour of arrival.
Restore flow first with a temporary vascular shunt, before skeletal stabilisation and definitive vascular reconstruction.
Reduce and stabilise the skeleton immediately after reperfusion, before definitive revascularisation.
Reconstruct with arterial repair or an interposition graft; reserve bypass for blast or ballistic injury, or when anatomical reconstruction is not feasible.
Always consider fasciotomy after revascularisation, and document the name of the senior decision-maker if it is not done.
Any decision for early amputation is made by two consultants from different specialties and documented.
Children with a supracondylar humeral fracture, no palpable radial pulse but a well-perfused hand: observation rather than immediate vascular intervention may be appropriate.
Vascular surgical technique, shunt use and the role of endovascular repair are set out in the ESVS vascular trauma guideline.

escalate.text: Consultant-led orthopaedic care plus vascular or plastic surgery is mandatory once an arterial injury is confirmed.
No vascular service on site: transfer is part of the revascularisation clock, so call before the CT is reported.
After repair, nurse where staff can assess a critically injured limb, and consider single antiplatelet therapy after a bleeding-risk assessment.

notes: Order of operations: shunt, then skeleton, then definitive vessel. Fixing the bone first while the limb waits is the classic error.
Reperfusion causes swelling. A compartment that was soft before the shunt may not be soft an hour after it.
When cognition allows, tell the patient early that amputation is a possible outcome.
